content: Sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) is characterized by the sudden and unexplained death of an infant, typically occurring without any prior symptoms. It most commonly affects infants between the ages of one month and one year in the United States. Women who have experienced the loss of an infant due to SIDS are at a significantly increased risk of complications in subsequent pregnancies. These complications may include placenta previa, abruptio placentae, and premature rupture of membranes. The prognosis for SIDS varies depending on the presence of risk factors for recurrence. These risk factors may include a history of apparent life-threatening events (ALTE), multiple preceding events requiring hospital admission, and viral infections. Such factors play a critical role in determining the likelihood of recurrence and overall prognosis in cases of SIDS.
